name: Apache Flink
summary: The most widely used open-source engine for stateful stream processing: keyed state, event time and exactly-once recovery from checkpoints.
intro: A Flink job is a graph of operators (sources, maps, joins, windows, sinks) written in SQL, the Table API, the Java DataStream API or Python. A client hands the graph to the JobManager, which splits each operator into parallel subtasks and schedules them into the task slots of the TaskManager processes. Records are routed by key, so every event for one key reaches the same subtask, and that subtask keeps the key’s state: on the Java heap by default, in RocksDB on local disk for state bigger than memory, or, since Flink 2.0, experimentally in ForSt, which keeps state in object storage such as S3 with a local cache. Windows close by event time: a watermark says how far the event clock has got. To survive failures, the JobManager regularly injects checkpoint barriers at the sources; as they flow through the graph, each operator snapshots its state, and the source offsets are stored alongside it in durable storage. After a crash the job restarts from the last checkpoint and rereads the input from those offsets, and transactional sinks such as Kafka make the output exactly once. A savepoint is the same snapshot taken by hand, used to upgrade code or change parallelism.

Flink is an Apache project under Apache 2.0, and runs as a standalone cluster, on YARN or on Kubernetes, where the Flink Kubernetes Operator manages jobs as custom resources. Flink 2.0 (March 2025) was the first major release in nine years: it added disaggregated state and removed long-deprecated APIs such as DataSet and the Scala APIs; 2.3 followed in June 2026. Running it yourself is free but takes work, so three companies sell it as a service: AWS (Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, called Kinesis Data Analytics until 2023), Confluent (Confluent Cloud for Apache Flink, SQL over its Kafka topics) and Ververica, the company Flink’s creators founded, now with its own Flink-compatible engine.
strengths: Large, exactly-once state: keyed state can outgrow memory (RocksDB, or ForSt on object storage), and checkpoints store it together with the source offsets
Real event-time processing: watermarks, tumbling, sliding and session windows, timers and a CEP library for patterns across events
Savepoints let you stop a job, change its code or parallelism, and resume from exactly where it was
One engine for streams and bounded batch input, with SQL, Java and Python APIs on top
The widest ecosystem in stream processing: Kafka, Kinesis, Iceberg, Paimon, database change capture through Flink CDC, and three managed services
limits: Running it is a job in itself: JobManager high availability, checkpoint storage, state backend and memory tuning, and upgrades through savepoints
Flink 2.x broke compatibility: state from 1.x isn’t guaranteed to restore, and the DataSet API, Scala APIs and old `SourceFunction`/`SinkFunction` connectors are gone
Connectors ship separately and lag the core: in October 2026 the Kafka connector supports Flink up to 2.2 and the AWS (Kinesis) connectors only 2.0, while Flink itself is at 2.3
Disaggregated state (ForSt) is still experimental, and Amazon’s managed service doesn’t offer it, or materialized tables
JVM first: Python user-defined functions run in separate Python processes by default, paying for serialization between the two

sections.title: Ways to run Flink in 2026
sections.intro: The same open-source engine, run by you or by one of three vendors. List prices checked 2026-10-06.
columns: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

rows.label: Who runs it
values: You: a standalone cluster, YARN, or Kubernetes with the Flink Kubernetes Operator
AWS: serverless applications that scale in KPUs (1 vCPU and 4 GB each)
Confluent: serverless compute pools that scale between zero and a cap you set
Ververica’s control plane in your AWS, Azure or GCP account (BYOC), or self-managed on any Kubernetes

rows.label: How you write jobs
values: SQL, Table API, DataStream API (Java), Python
Java or Python applications; Studio notebooks (Apache Zeppelin) for interactive SQL and Python
Flink SQL; Table API in Java (generally available) and Python (preview)
Apache Flink APIs, SQL and connectors, run on Ververica’s own VERA engine, which it says is fully compatible

rows.label: Versions and gaps
values: Flink 2.3, 2.2, 1.20, 1.19, 1.18 and 1.15; no ForSt state backend, materialized tables or Java 21
Managed by Confluent; every Kafka topic in the region appears as a table, and queries can’t cross regions
Ververica claims twice the throughput of open-source Flink; not independently verified here

rows.label: Price
values: Free (Apache 2.0); you pay for machines, storage and people
$0.11 per KPU-hour in us-east-1, plus one extra KPU per application for orchestration, plus $0.10 per GB-month of running storage (50 GB per KPU)
$0.21 per CFU-hour (varies by region), billed by the minute, at least 1 CFU-minute per statement; Kafka networking charged as usual

notes: On AWS, a small always-on application with one KPU is billed for two (one is for orchestration): about $160 a month, plus about $5 for its 50 GB of running storage.
Confluent bills the CFUs statements actually use, not the pool’s maximum size; a Baseline CFU setting makes a statement pay for a floor even when idle.

sections.title: What changed in Flink 2.x
sections.intro: Flink 2.0 ended the 1.x compatibility promise that had held since 2016. The main changes, and what they mean for an upgrade:

items.name: Disaggregated state
items.text: The ForSt state backend keeps state in a distributed file system such as S3 or HDFS, with local disk only as a cache, and operators read it asynchronously. State size is no longer capped by the TaskManager’s disk, and recovery doesn’t have to download the state first. Turned on with `state.backend.type: forst`; not every SQL operator supports it yet.

items.name: Removed APIs
items.text: The DataSet API, the Scala DataStream and DataSet APIs, `SourceFunction`, `SinkFunction`, Sink V1 and the legacy `TableSource`/`TableSink` are gone. Connectors built on them had to be rewritten, and `flink-conf.yaml` was replaced by a standard `config.yaml`.

items.name: No state compatibility from 1.x
items.text: Savepoints from 1.x aren’t guaranteed to restore in 2.x, so stateful jobs may need to rebuild their state. Java 17 became the default, Java 8 support was dropped, and the per-job deployment mode was removed in favour of application mode.

items.name: Materialized tables
items.text: A table defined by a query that Flink keeps refreshed, choosing streaming or batch execution itself, with Apache Paimon as the supported catalog. Flink 2.3 added explicit column definitions and a `START_MODE` clause, so a changed query doesn’t always reprocess history.

items.name: Flink 2.3
items.text: SQL gained `FROM_CHANGELOG` and `TO_CHANGELOG` for converting between append-only streams and changelogs, and an `ON CONFLICT` clause that forces a choice when the upsert key differs from the sink’s primary key. A native S3 filesystem on AWS SDK v2 arrived as an experiment.

story: In 2009 researchers at the Technical University of Berlin started Stratosphere, a research project to build the next generation of big data analytics platform. Its motto was “write like a programming language, execute like a database”: it mixed ideas from MapReduce and parallel databases, and managed its own memory as binary data instead of piling Java objects on the heap.

Stratosphere’s engine entered the Apache Incubator as Flink in April 2014 and graduated in December. The same year its core developers, among them Kostas Tzoumas and Stephan Ewen, founded data Artisans in Berlin to build a business around it, and in 2015 they turned Flink towards stream processing. Version 0.10 (November 2015) brought event time, out-of-order streams and exactly-once recovery; 1.0 (March 2016) added RocksDB state and savepoints. Alibaba, which ran its own fork called Blink, bought data Artisans for €90 million in January 2019 and contributed Blink back to the project; the company is now called Ververica.

Flink became the default open-source engine for stateful streaming, and cloud providers built services on it: AWS added Flink to Kinesis Data Analytics in 2018 and renamed the service after Flink in 2023. Flink 2.0, in March 2025, was the first major release in nine years.

choices.choice: Streams first, batch as a stream that ends
choices.why: If an engine can process unbounded streams continuously, bounded data sets are just streams that stop. Building on that idea let one runtime and, over time, one API serve both real-time and historical processing.

choices.choice: Asynchronous barrier snapshots for fault tolerance
choices.why: Earlier approaches either paused the computation to take a global snapshot or saved every in-flight record. Barriers that flow with the data let each operator snapshot only its own state without stopping, which Flink’s developers described in a 2015 paper.

choices.choice: Managing its own memory as binary data
choices.why: From its database roots, Flink serialized records into pre-allocated memory segments and ran sort and join algorithms directly on the bytes. That avoided out-of-memory crashes and heavy garbage collection on large JVM heaps, and let operators spill to disk predictably.
Events often arrive late and out of order. Grouping by when things happened, with watermarks marking progress, gives the same results on live data and on a replay, which 0.10 made a core feature.
